commits.message:
fix(core): run web terminal PTYs on the bundled ConPTY backend (#11643)

* fix(core): run web terminal PTYs on the bundled ConPTY backend

The web terminal spawned its PTYs with node-pty's default inbox ConPTY
backend, where a natural shell exit orphans the conhost.exe --headless
the backend spawned: the native exit watcher erases the pty baton before
delivering onExit, pty_baton has no destructor, and the erased HPCON is
unreachable from JS (microsoft/node-pty#965). Every exited web terminal
leaked ~8 MB for the life of the CLI, and a pin bump does not fix it.

Mirror the #11497 shell path: spawn with useConptyDll on Windows so the
bundled backend releases its host reference right after spawn and the
host exits with its last client. The bundled backend adds one
synchronous throw point — a missing or unloadable conpty.dll — and a
web terminal has no child_process fallback, so a failed bundled spawn
retries once on the inbox backend: the pre-fix leaking behavior beats a
terminal that cannot start at all. A failed spawn produced no child, so
the retry cannot double-spawn. The 4001 non-retryable close path is
unchanged.

Also switch the agent-view PTY host to the bundled backend (same leak,
lower rate), refresh the conpty-host release docs, and add a
VERIFIED_NODE_PTY pin test so a node-pty bump forces re-verification of
the native teardown semantics the release path depends on.

Refs #11352

* fix(core): derive node-pty pins and widen the conpty-host pin guard

The six `@lydell/node-pty*` pins live in three unsynchronized places — the
root manifest, packages/core's manifest, and a hardcoded map in
scripts/prepare-package.js — but the conpty-host tripwire asserted only
one key of one manifest, so bumping the win32 prebuild keys or the root
manifest left it green and skipped the human re-check it exists to force.

Derive the six pins in writeDistPackageJson from packages/core's manifest
(deleting the third hardcoded table), and widen the tripwire to assert all
six core keys plus an equality against the root manifest's six — the
declaration packages/cli's agent-view actually resolves in a dev tree.

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>
Patrol-Run: qwen-pr-closeout/jmtxennouyn

* fix(core): answer and scrub bundled-backend terminal queries in the web terminal

Switching the web-terminal registry to the bundled ConPTY backend let a
probing shell's DA / DSR query bytes into the recorded scrollback; a
reconnect that replays the buffer made the client's xterm.js re-answer
each query and write the fresh reply back into the still-live shell's
stdin. The bundled backend answers no queries itself, and the browser is
not guaranteed to be attached when the startup probe fires.

Mirror the other half of the shell path (#11497): on win32, feed a
headless terminal the PTY stream so it answers the probe server-side, and
strip the query bytes from both the scrollback and the live stream so a
replay cannot re-emit them. Also bring the releasePtyResources docstring
in line with the bundled backend (R1-8).

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>
Patrol-Run: qwen-pr-closeout/jmtxennouyn

* fix(core): close query-strip gaps and a race in the web terminal

Three review findings on the bundled-ConPTY web terminal path:

- The scrollback scrub was a stateless per-chunk regex over only the `c`/`n`
  finals, so the query families xterm.js answers beyond those (tertiary DA,
  DECRQM, DECRQSS, XTVERSION, DECREQTPARM, OSC colour queries) still reached
  the scrollback and were re-answered into the live shell on reconnect. Replace
  it with a stateful stripper covering every family and carrying a probe split
  across two chunks.

- resize() resized only session.pty, leaving the headless query responder on
  its 80x24 spawn grid, so geometry-dependent replies were computed against
  the wrong size. Forward the resize to session.queryTerminal.

- loadXtermHeadless() was a second suspension point whose cancelledCreations/
  disposed guards were not re-checked, so a release()/releaseWorkspace()/
  dispose() landing during the import leaked a PTY the caller had cancelled.
  Re-check both after the import.

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>
Patrol-Run: qwen-pr-closeout/jmtxrimarz8

* fix(core): strip DCS DECRQSS queries in the terminal query filter

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>

Patrol-Run: qwen-pr-closeout/jmty6iqs0zv

* fix(core): bound the terminal query stripper and tie it to its responder

The stateful stripper held any unterminated OSC (a title SET included) with no cap, so one stray ESC ] swallowed every later chunk and grew pending unbounded; the DCS alternative also required the full introducer, leaking its halves that reassemble into a re-answered DECRQSS. Hold only viable query prefixes, cap the hold, end an OSC partial at a bare ESC (accepting the C1 ST terminator), hold the DCS introducer, and gate the stripper on the responder so a failed headless load no longer strips with nobody left to answer. Correct the query-set doc comment.

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>
Patrol-Run: qwen-pr-closeout/jmtyf3dx109

* style(core): format web-terminal-registry.ts with prettier

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>
Patrol-Run: qwen-pr-conflict/jmtyhy9mj0e

* fix(web-terminal): stop scrubbing the OSC colour family the server cannot answer

The stateful stripper added here removed the OSC 10/11/12/4 colour queries from
both the scrollback and the live listener, but the pinned @xterm/headless 5.5.0
responder answers none of them: `onData` carries DA/DSR/DECRQM/DECRQSS only,
while `_setOrReportSpecialColor` reports on the internal `_onColor` emitter that
the headless Terminal does not expose (`term.onColor` is undefined) and that
nothing in this file subscribes to. Deleting the family from the browser's
stream as well left a probing program unanswered, where the browser's own
xterm.js 6.0.0 `_handleColorEvent` is the answerer and answered it at the merge
base.

Narrow both regexes to the families the responder actually answers (plus the
never-display-content DA3 / XTVERSION / DECREQTPARM trio that no build answers),
drop the half-covered colour arm from the partial matcher — so the strip set and
the doc block no longer disagree about what the colour family is — and correct
the doc block to state the split. Covered by a new test asserting the whole
family reaches both the live listener and the snapshot untouched, and that
nothing is written back; it fails if the colour arm is restored.

The colour queries that a reconnect replay re-answers are part of the
replay-suppression redesign tracked in #11734.

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>
Patrol-Run: qwen-pr-closeout/jmtyno0zh0n

* fix(web-terminal): separate live replies from reconnect history

Preserve raw PTY bytes and limit the Windows server responder to primary DA. Mark snapshots explicitly and restore history into a detached browser terminal while the old terminal continues forwarding user input. Activate live replies at the snapshot write callback, reject incompatible peers, and preserve the parallel color-query regression fix. Refs #11734.

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>

fix(lsp): synchronize target documents before queries (#11443)

* fix(lsp): synchronize target documents before queries

* fix(lsp): address document synchronization review findings

* fix(lsp): address second-round document synchronization review findings

Evict an un-synchronizable document where the throw is raised, so one
deleted or unsupported file stops being fatal for the rest of the
connection, while workspace synchronization failures still escape the
ordinary pull-request catch instead of returning partial success.

Certify a prepare result that points at another file by observing that
file inside the synchronous signing loop, where no await separates the
response from the observation. The documented prepare-then-traverse
workflow no longer fails closed on a fresh cross-file item, and it costs
no notification, no settle delay and no second round trip. Nested items
whose own file drifted stay unsigned without dropping healthy siblings,
non-file items report non-retryable guidance, and tokens bind a text
digest plus delivered version rather than the whole document.

An unreadable warmup probe no longer cancels workspace symbol search, and
the manager only blames the synchronization callback when the server's
capabilities really cannot accept a notification.

Both design docs now define each mutation gate inline instead of citing
identifiers that resolve to nothing in the tree.

feat(goal): rerun a stalled checkpoint in batches, smaller after each stall (#11690)

* feat(goal): rerun a stalled checkpoint in batches, smaller after each stall

A checkpoint that stalls on an overflowing window leaves the cursor where
it was, so the next attempt rebuilt the same window and sent the verifier
the identical request at temperature 0, failing the same way until the
stall breaker stopped the Goal.

The first check on a window still sends it whole. A check that starts with
a stall streak splits the evidence into consecutive batches (24 records
after one stall, 12 after two) and calls the verifier once per batch:

- each batch's claims are carried into the next as previousClaims, and
  only the last batch's checkpoint is kept and moves the cursor;
- intermediate batches use their own claim id segment (<uuid>:b<k>:<n>);
- a failing batch ends the check through the existing arms, and the
  recorded failure names the batch ("batch 2/5: ...") inside the cap;
- a restore replay batches by its restored streak and still spends no
  stall.

Docs describe the batching and its worst-case duration, and the
goalCheckpointTimeoutSeconds description says the ceiling is per call.

* fix(goal): split only an overflowing live checkpoint, not a room window or a replay

A window with room settles a failed check as inconclusive and a restore
replay is exempt from the stall breaker, so neither can spend a stall and
splitting them bought nothing: it only added verifier calls and lossy
per-batch recompression, and for a replay held up session activation,
which waits for the replay to finish. Both now go out in one call as they
did before; only a live check on an overflowing window after a stall is
split.

feat(workflows): add effort and disallowedTools to agent() options (#11691)

* feat(workflows): add effort and disallowedTools to agent() options

A workflow script can now set the reasoning effort for one agent and take
tools away from it. Every agent previously ran at the session's effort with
the full tool set minus a fixed floor, so a script paid high-effort cost on
cheap stages or ran its judges at low effort, and a read-only stage could
still edit files.

agent({ effort }) accepts low, medium, high, xhigh or max with the aliases
/effort accepts, and omitting it inherits the session tier. The tier goes
onto the agent's own copy of the content-generator config, never the
session's, limited to the tiers /effort offers for that model: a tier the
model does not offer becomes the next stronger one it does, and a model
offering none keeps the inherited tier. It is written by the session
setter's logic, now one shared helper, and providers still clamp it per
request. An effort-only dispatch gets its own runtime view for that reason.

agent({ disallowedTools }) is unioned with the workflow floor and the agent
type's own denies, so it only narrows. Display names resolve through the
spawn's normalizer. A schema agent that denies structured_output is refused
before it spawns.

Both options join the resume key. The sandbox validates and normalizes them
on the revived copy that crosses to the host (alias to tier, deny list
sorted and de-duplicated), so equivalent spellings replay and different
requests run live. The workflow-authoring skill documents both.

Part of #11013

* fix(workflows): make per-agent effort and deny lists hold

Address the first review round of the agent() effort and
disallowedTools options.

Effort: an explicit tier now drops a thinking budget the agent's copy
inherited, never re-enables thinking the session turned off (also across
a provider switch), finds the declared tiers behind a gateway base URL,
and falls back to the provider's built-in tier table when the registry
declares none. An effort-only dispatch builds its own generator only
when the tier can land, refuses to open an interactive login for it, and
runs on the session's generator if that build fails. The CLI's /effort
tier rule now delegates to the same core helper.

Deny lists: an entry that matches no tool is refused instead of silently
denying nothing, built-in display names become tool names before the
resume key is derived, and a schema agent is refused when any deny in
the union reaching the spawn, including its agent type's own, names
structured_output. The fast path is driven by the option list the resume
key projects.

Sandbox: the phase is recorded only after the option gates pass, and an
echoed effort value is stripped of control characters. The review
harness mirror accepts the two options, and the authoring skill states
where effort does not reach.

Part of #11013

fix(core): guard internal git calls against configured helper programs (#11669)

* fix(core): stop a repository's own git config from running programs during automatic git calls

A repository can name a program in its own .git/config and have git run it
on the next index refresh. The git calls the agent makes on its own
initiative reached that: startup context, the daemon's working-tree status
and diffs, the ignore probe, the grep tool, the team-memory sync, the
stale-worktree sweep, and the two worktree dialogs.

Guard at the chokepoints (the simple-git factory, gitDiff's runGit, the
team-memory and orphan-cleanup spawn points) with -c core.fsmonitor=, and
pass --no-ext-diff --no-textconv on the diff calls for the two
program-valued keys that config cannot empty.

* test(core): mock execFileSync in chatRecordingService tests

getGitBranch now calls execFileSync instead of execSync, so the tests' node:child_process mock must stub execFileSync to keep gitBranch resolving to 'main'.

hasWorktreeChanges and countWorktreeChanges passed GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0
through simple-git's two-arg .env(), which replaces the child environment

safe.directory. Run the status probe through execFile with
`-c core.fsmonitor= --no-optional-locks status --porcelain` instead, so the

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>
Patrol-Run: qwen-pr-closeout/jmty28f6zzp

* fix(core): suppress post-index-change on the team-memory status probe and roll back on rejected push

The session-start status probe in syncTeamMemory lacked --no-optional-locks,
so when the team path is clean it was the flow's only index-writing call and a

rejected commit then stranded on the branch and tripped wasAheadBeforeSync,

Add real-git regressions for both: a clean-path post-index-change canary, and a
pre-receive-rejecting remote asserting HEAD is restored and a second sync does

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>

* fix(core): close remaining git config exec and rollback gaps

- Team-memory push-failure rollback now rewinds by SHA: it records the

refactor(core): apply one matcher rule to every hook event (#11619)

* refactor(core): apply one matcher rule to every hook event

Hook matchers meant different things per event and per registration
path. Notification, PreCompact, PostCompact and StopFailure accepted only
a single exact value, so `permission_prompt|idle_prompt` never matched,
and session-scoped hooks, including skill frontmatter hooks, anchored
their regex while settings hooks did not.

One shared matchesHookPattern now serves the planner and the session
hooks manager: an empty matcher, `*` or `.*` matches everything; the
matcher or any entry of a `|` list matches exactly (tool events also
compare aliases exactly); otherwise it is an unanchored regex on the
subject. Existing tool, subagent, command, session and file-path matcher
behaviour is unchanged.

Part of #11610

* fix(core): decide pipe-list matchers entry by entry

Review follow-up. A `|` list compared its entries exactly and then fell
back to the whole pattern as a regex, so `Write|*` became an invalid
regex that matched nothing, and a stray pipe such as `write_file|edit|`
became a regex that matched everything. Lists are now decided entry by
entry with the full rule; empty entries are ignored and never widen the
list, and a group spanning the pipe such as `a(b|c)` still falls back to
one regex.

The planner no longer keeps its own copy of the match-all rule. The hooks
and skills guides now say that skill matchers are unanchored, that an
omitted skill matcher matches every tool, how to anchor runtime ids and
exclusions, and that aliases only match exactly.

Part of #11610

* fix(core): decide pipe-list matcher entries without compiling them

A pipe-list entry now matches only as `*`, `.*`, or an exact subject or
alias. Entries are no longer compiled one by one, so an escaped pipe such
as `notes\|todo\.md` keeps its whole-pattern meaning instead of letting
the `todo\.md` fragment match any path, and a group that spans the pipe
no longer logs "Invalid regex" warnings for its unbalanced fragments.

The whole-pattern fall-through is compiled from the non-empty entries, so
a stray `|` is dropped rather than disabling the fall-through:
`read_(file|edit)|` matches `read_file`, while a list of only `|` still
matches nothing and a trailing `|` never becomes a match-all.

Pin that a skill hook entry without `matcher:` matches every tool.

* fix(core): trim pipe-list matcher entries and split only on unescaped pipes

Trim each list entry at the split so the exact comparison and the rebuilt
regular expression see the same entries: `read_.* | edit` now matches
`read_file` instead of compiling alternatives that demand literal spaces.

Split only on a `|` that is not preceded by a backslash, so an escaped pipe
never manufactures an empty entry or a dangling escape: `notes\|` matches
`x/notes|y`, `a\||b` matches `b`, and `foo\|bar` no longer matches `bar`.

Scope the documented stray-pipe guarantee to lists that do not start with
`^` or `(`; those matchers are compiled as written.

* fix(core): split matcher lists only at top-level pipes

The list reading of a matcher split on every pipe not preceded by a
backslash, so it cut through character classes and groups and then trimmed
spaces that belonged to the expression: `foo[ |]bar` was rebuilt as
`foo[|]bar` and stopped matching `foo bar`, and `a(b | c)` lost its spaces
the same way. A single preceding backslash also hid a real separator after
an escaped backslash, so `C:\\temp\\|D:\\data\\|` kept its trailing empty
alternative and matched everything.

Split with a scan that reads backslashes in pairs and ignores pipes inside
`[...]` and groups, so only top-level entries are trimmed, compared and
rebuilt, and `read_.* | edit` keeps reading as `read_.*|edit`. Tests pin
each shape and the `^` and `(` guards, and the hooks guide says which pipes
separate entries.

fix(core): fire active-todo reminders at delegation boundaries and user turns (#10963)

* fix(core): fire active-todo reminders at delegation boundaries and user turns

A session that delegates to foreground subagents earns one parent tool
turn per tens of minutes of real work, so the 3-turn budget of the
active-todo reminder never comes due and the persisted plan freezes
(#10953). Any ordinary user turn additionally discards a registered
reminder, so the very message asking about progress destroys the plan
context.

- Force the reminder due on a tool-result batch that carries a
  top-level Agent tool result, in both the TUI (client.ts) and ACP
  (Session.ts) paths, putting the nudge exactly where delegated
  progress arrives.
- Continue the previous work chain on an ordinary user turn while a
  reminder is still registered — a registered reminder implies
  unfinished items, since todo_write deletes it on plan completion.
  This mirrors the existing retry continuation.

The observational contract of todo_id is unchanged. Time-aware cadence
(direction c) and the delayed tool-response recording (direction e) are
separate concerns and intentionally not included.

Co-authored-by: Qwen-Coder <qwen-coder@alibabacloud.com>
Patrol-Run: qwen-issue-patrol/jmtlu4sumgg

* docs(design): sync active-todo-context with the two rules this PR changes

The doc still promised that an ordinary new prompt clears stale Todo state,
and described the turn cadence as the reminder's only delivery path. This PR
changes both: an ordinary turn continues the chain while a reminder is
registered, and a tool-result batch carrying a top-level Agent result forces
the reminder due because a delegated run earns the parent a single turn.

Record the accepted cost (an abandoned plan resurfaces until a later write
completes or clears it) and that the ACP todo-stop-guard lineage reset stays
keyed to the retry/continue flag, so carrying a plan never widens guard trust.

* fix(core): clear stale active-todo reminders on rewind and preserve automatic-turn owners

History rewind / restore / setHistory discard the timeline the active-todo
reminder describes, but the reminder and its work-chain owner survived, so the
next turn continued work that was rewound away. Clear the reminder state where
history is discarded (LlmClient.truncateHistory/setHistory, ACP
rewindToTurn/restoreHistory) via a new Config.clearActiveTodoReminders().

Continuing a chain also dropped still-live related automatic turns' owner
mappings (owners.clear()), so a plan completed by an in-flight automatic turn
kept its reminder and kept reporting unfinished work. Re-point instead of
clearing, dropping only entries whose mapped owner is discarded.

Extend the continuation tests to pin the cleared-reminder branch, parameterize

fix(core): compute cron next-fire time with epoch arithmetic across DST fall-back (#11723)

nextFireTime advanced its minute-by-minute scan with local Date setters
(setSeconds / setMinutes). ECMA-262 resolves an ambiguous fall-back
wall-clock to its earlier occurrence, so an anchor inside the repeated
autumn hour was re-projected up to 59 minutes into the past, breaking the
strictly-after contract, and a forward scan skipped the entire second
occurrence of the hour.

Traverse elapsed time instead: initialise the candidate with epoch
arithmetic (floor(after/60000)*60000 + 60000) and advance with
candidate.setTime(candidate.getTime() + 60000), while continuing to match
cron fields with local getters. Cron syntax, jitter policy, and other
scheduler behavior are unchanged. Fixes the root cause reported in #11720.

fix(core): reap surviving hook process trees on Windows (#11623)

* fix(core): reap surviving hook process trees on Windows

terminateSurvivingHookProcessGroup was an explicit no-op on win32, so
when a parent-exit-surviving hook (MessageDisplay / StopFailure /
SessionDelete) was cancelled, nothing reaped the shell the supervisor had
started. Those hooks spawn a detached supervisor plus a shell child and
unref() it, so the parent's own tree kill on the supervisor is not a
reliable substitute: the supervisor may already have exited, which
reparents the shell out of its tree, or its taskkill may fail. The result
is the leftover cmd.exe processes reported in #11303.

Implement the branch with taskkill /f /t, extracted from
terminateWindowsHookProcessTree as a shared pid-only helper.

Guarded by a process.kill(pid, 0) liveness probe first. Windows has no
process group to signal, so an unguarded taskkill against a pid that has
already exited could land on a recycled pid belonging to an unrelated
application — the #6067 collateral-kill failure mode. The POSIX branch
gets that safety for free by signalling the negated pid.

* fix(core): reuse shared pid liveness probe in Windows surviving-hook reap

* fix(core): warn when a surviving-hook liveness probe fails unexpectedly

An unexpected process.kill(pid, 0) errno (ENOMEM, EMFILE, libuv's
UV_UNKNOWN catch-all, ...) read as "dead" through isPidAlive, so the
Windows surviving-hook reap skipped without a trace even though the
hook's cmd.exe tree may still be running. Classify the probe at the
call site into alive/gone/unknown — the skip decision is unchanged —
and warn on the unknown case.

Also pin that the win32 branch never falls through to the POSIX
process-group path with a negative-pid assertion, and record the warn
in the design docs.

* fix(core): size code-mode host startup grace for slow machines

A code-mode execution's wall clock is timeoutMs +
CODE_MODE_HOST_STARTUP_GRACE_MS, measured from host spawn. A 5s grace
is below the observed cold boot of the host process (node + tsx +
QuickJS WASM init, ~4s unloaded and worse under parallel load) on slow
machines, so executions with a small timeoutMs were killed during boot
with a spurious "timed out" error. Raise the grace to 30s, matching
the guest timeout scale; fast machines see no change since the
deadline only binds when startup is slow.

Also lift two scheduler tests' intermediate vi.waitFor budgets (4s)
and one exec-context test's (1s default) to 30s: nested tool dispatch
cannot be observed before the host has booted, so deadlines below the
boot time failed deterministically on slow runners. Assertions are
unchanged; each test's own timeout still caps it.

* fix(core): sharpen surviving-hook probe diagnostics and code-mode timeout message

- Carry the probe errno in the surviving-hook skip warning and share the
  tri-state liveness classification with the SIGKILL-fallback re-probe,
  which now warns instead of skipping silently on an unexpected errno.
- Report the wall budget actually enforced (guest budget + host startup
  grace) when the code-mode host never frames a response.
- Raise the enclosing per-test caps above the 30s waitFor budgets so a
  genuine stall still surfaces the assertion diff, and state in the
  design docs that the probe warnings live in the debug log (--debug).

fix(vscode): shut the ACP CLI down gracefully instead of killing it (#11642)

* fix(vscode): shut the ACP CLI down gracefully instead of killing it

disconnect() used to child.kill() the CLI: TerminateProcess on Windows
(cleanup never runs, MCP/PTY/conhost children orphaned — the teardown
half of #11303) and a bare SIGTERM on POSIX with no bound. Now stdin is
closed so the CLI runs its own shutdown (SessionEnd hooks, MCP pool
drain, session dispose, exit-time reaper), with a bounded escalation
behind it: 45s grace sized from the CLI's own drain budgets, then a
process-group SIGTERM (catchable, runs the signal cleanup), then SIGKILL
after 10s. Windows goes straight to a taskkill tree kill once the grace
expires, since console processes have no catchable terminate.

Replacing the current session (session/new, session/load) now also
closes the superseded one — a retained session keeps firing autonomous
turns when its background tasks complete, which is what grew conhost.exe
without bound in #11303. The close is conditional (onlyIfUnheld) with an
8s drain budget, and refused/failed closes retry on a 60s doubling
backoff capped at 1h, so in-flight work is never dropped and the leak
stays tracked. The CLI side of that close path gets the matching
concurrency idempotency: a SIGTERM landing mid-ide_close now joins the
in-flight MCP pool drain and session dispose instead of running them
twice.

Superseded connections can no longer tear down the live one: child
handlers bind their own child, inbound callbacks and stale request
resolutions check against the connection they were wired on.

fix(core)!: read command hook timeout in seconds (#11615)

* fix(core)!: read command hook timeout in seconds with a 600s default

Command hooks passed `timeout` to the timer as milliseconds, while HTTP
and prompt hooks read it as seconds, the settings schema described
seconds, and the hooks guide documented both. A command hook written
with `"timeout": 10` was killed after 10ms and failed open.

Command hook `timeout` is now read in seconds and defaults to 600s. A
value of 1000 or more is still read as milliseconds so existing settings
keep their meaning, and a debug-log warning names each such hook once.
Timeout errors report seconds. HTTP, prompt and function hooks are
unchanged. The schema description, generated JSON schema and every
command hook example in the guide now use seconds.

BREAKING CHANGE: a command hook `timeout` below 1000 is now seconds
rather than milliseconds.

Part of #11610

* fix(core): keep hook timeouts authoritative and surface legacy values

Review follow-up.

- Hook execution requests on the message bus no longer carry the bus's
  60-second default deadline, so a hook is bounded by its own timeout
  instead of being abandoned while it keeps running. Explicit caller
  timeouts and other request types are unchanged.
- Command hooks on MessageDisplay, StopFailure and SessionDelete, which
  outlive the CLI, default to 60 seconds instead of 600.
- Settings warnings now name each command hook whose timeout is still
  read as milliseconds; the advice never suggests a seconds value that
  would itself be read as milliseconds.
- The hooks guide scopes "seconds" to command, HTTP and prompt hooks and
  notes async slot usage; shipped external-context examples use seconds.
- Tests pin the async registration and supervisor deadlines, and reset
  the warning deduplication between cases.

Part of #11610

* docs(core): explain long command hook timeouts and blocking hold time

A command hook timeout of 1000 or more is still read as legacy
milliseconds, so a value meant as a long timeout in seconds, such as 1800
for 30 minutes, ends up as 1.8 seconds. The startup warning now also says
how to keep the value that was meant as seconds, and the hooks guide
explains that long timeouts stay in milliseconds. The guide also notes that
a synchronous hook on an event that waits for its result holds the turn
until it exits or times out, 600 seconds by default.

* fix(core): bound signal-less hook requests and cancel tool hooks on abort

The message bus now waives its default deadline only for hook execution
requests that carry an abort signal. Requests without one cannot be
cancelled, so they keep the 60-second deadline instead of waiting on the
hook's own timeout.

PreToolUse, PostToolUse and non-interrupt PostToolUseFailure hooks now
receive the tool's abort signal, in the payload and as the request signal,
so an abort stops the hook and releases the wait. Interrupt reports keep no
signal because it is already aborted there. The UserPromptSubmit hook gets
the send signal, and a send aborted during or right after that hook ends as
an abort instead of recording or sending the prompt.

MessageDisplay deliveries pass the turn signal to the request, warn when the
bus reports a failed hook execution, and stay quiet when the turn was
cancelled.

A command hook timeout written as a numeric string is read like the number
it holds instead of falling back to the default.

The startup warning for legacy millisecond timeouts is removed from this
change and tracked in #11675; the hooks guide now explains how to find such
hooks. Async hook timeout messages report seconds, the remaining first-party
millisecond values in integration fixtures and design docs are rewritten in
seconds, and the async hooks bullet names the 60-second default on events
whose hooks outlive the process.

* fix(core): keep the 60 second command hook default and drop hook bus signal threading

Raising the command hook default to 600 seconds forced two rounds of
reconciliation with the 60 second and 15 second bus deadlines: first by
waiving the deadline, then by threading abort signals through the tool
and prompt hook call sites. Each round produced new regressions (payload
vs request signal, already-aborted failure reports, unmigrated arity
assertions, orphaned hook children, cancels recorded as hook errors). The
default change and the cancellation work move to a follow-up issue, and
this change keeps only the unit.

- Command hook timeouts stay in seconds with a 60 second default, the
  same duration as before; values of 1000 or more keep their legacy
  millisecond meaning, and numeric strings are still coerced. The
  separate default for hooks that outlive the process is gone because it
  now equals the default.
- MessageBus, tool hook triggers, the scheduler, the UserPromptSubmit
  request, the MessageDisplay dispatcher and their tests are back to main.
- An unusable timeout such as "30s" is named in the debug log with the
  default it was replaced by, like a legacy millisecond value.
- Timeout warnings are recorded as sent only once debug logging can write
  them, and are deduplicated per session.
- Async hook timeout messages and a real spawned hook with timeout 1 now
  pin the seconds conversion.

feat(core): auto-retry transient network errors (EOF) where Ctrl+Y is unavailable (#10347)

* feat(core): classify wrapped network failures (EOF) as retryable for bounded auto-retry

A 4xx that is actually a low-level network failure (e.g. '400 network error
... EOF', peer closed mid-request) was treated as a permanent client error
(fail-fast), so channel/daemon paths — which have no manual Ctrl+Y retry —
ended the turn on a transient fault. Recognize such wrapped failures (no
provider error body + EOF/transport cause) as retryable transport errors so
the existing bounded auto-retry (maxRetries + backoff) applies. Genuine
client 4xx with provider fields stay fail-fast.

Fixes #10346

* fix(core): retry 4xx-wrapped network failures on streaming turns (#10346)

The 4xx network-failure reclassification never reached the streaming
user-turn path: the establishment predicate rejected status 400 before
consulting the classifier, so the incident shape ("400 network error
for request ...: EOF") failed fast exactly as before this PR. Consult
the classification before the 400 rejection so provider-body-less
wrapped network failures get bounded retries while genuine client 400s
stay fail-fast.

Also restrict the classifier exception to that target: drop the
transport-code short-circuit so a 4xx carrying a socket code stays
fail-fast (restoring the pinned errorHandler invariant), and narrow the
message marker to the demonstrated wrapper shape so permanent client
errors that merely mention EOF are not retried. The classification
keeps reporting no transportCode, so these shapes stay out of the
transportCode-keyed mid-stream replay/continuation gates.

fix(acp-bridge): reject unlimited cgroup sentinel for ACP child heaps (#11653)

* fix(acp-bridge): reject unlimited cgroup sentinels when sizing ACP child heaps

The spawn path treated any positive `process.constrainedMemory()` as the memory
available to the daemon tree. libuv reports an absent cgroup limit as a huge
sentinel rather than as zero, so on a host with no limit configured every
spawned ACP child was authorised the full 16 GiB cap no matter how small the
machine was. On a 7265 MiB host each child received an old-space ceiling of
16384 MB — and because the flag is emitted only when it raises the ceiling, it
lifted that child above V8's own 2096 MB default instead of lowering anything.
The sentinel is reachable on cgroup v2 with no limit set, not only under
cgroup v1, so it is not the container-only edge case the previous comment
described.

Derive the figure from the detector the daemon's own status surface already
divides by, which rejects the sentinel and clamps to host memory. The spawn
path and the reported model no longer disagree by thirty-fold on the same
machine. The half-of-available fraction, the 16 GiB cap, the raise-only guard
and the memoized result are unchanged, so a real cgroup limit keeps the ceiling
it has today.

This is not a child-capacity policy: no spawn is refused, no ceiling is divided
by the child count, and the flag still bounds V8's old space rather than
process RSS.

Refs #8182

* test(acp-bridge): fold the saturated spawn-parity case into one file

The sibling parity file's header still described the two-file split as
avoiding a vi.resetModules() re-import, but the fraction file now does
exactly that per case — the only surviving statement of the split
rationale pointed future parity cases at the file with a static import
and no reset hook. Fold the saturated case into the fraction file's
it.each table (65_536 MB host, 4_096 MB heap limit, expecting
--max-old-space-size=16384) and delete the sibling, leaving one
canonical pattern for memoization-sensitive spawn-parity cases.

fix(core): report real stop_hook_active on Stop hooks (#11613)

* fix(core): report real stop_hook_active on Stop hooks

Both places that fire the Stop hook, the core client and the ACP session,
hard-coded stop_hook_active to true. A Stop hook that follows the usual
pattern of blocking only while stop_hook_active is false therefore never
blocked, and no hook could tell its own continuation apart.

The field is now false on the first stop check and true only when the
agent is continuing because a Stop hook blocked the previous stop, which
is what SubagentStop already reported. The core client derives it from
the stop hook iteration count it already threads into the continuation
turn; the ACP loop uses its own iteration counter.

Part of #11610

* fix(core): keep stop_hook_active across tool calls in a hook-forced chain

Review follow-up. The core client derived stop_hook_active and the
consecutive-block count from send options that only the internal
recursion carried, so a hook-forced continuation that called a tool came
back through a fresh call with the state lost: a guard-style hook
re-blocked forever and the blocking cap never fired. The next-speaker and
steer recursions, which spread the options, kept stale state instead.

The client now keeps the chain per prompt id, written by both blocking
branches and cleared when a stop is allowed, the cap is reached, the user
steers, or a Goal turn starts. The ACP loop reports the field from its
own flag, set only for continuations carrying a Stop hook reason and
cleared for drained user input, guard continuations and superseded ones,
leaving the iteration counter to the cap and continuation ids.

Tests cover a tool round trip, a next-speaker continuation, the
goal-bound branch, the guard reset sequence and a drained user turn.

Part of #11610

* fix(core): key stop_hook_active by prompt and keep the block count per call

Replace the single client-held Stop-hook chain with a set of prompt ids
whose previous Stop check was blocked. stop_hook_active reads that set,
so it still survives a tool round trip, while a second prompt stopping
on the same client (a concurrent side question) can no longer evict or
overwrite another prompt's state. An id is cleared when its stop is
allowed, the cap is hit, steer input replaces the turn, the send exits
abnormally, or a new interaction starts on that id (retry and goal turns
reuse the prompt id).

The consecutive-block count goes back to riding the per-call
stopHookState, as on main, so the built-in /goal hook stays bounded by
its own iteration budget. Counting blocks across tool round trips is
tracked in #11673.

In ACP, user input drained before or after a Stop check now also
restarts the consecutive-block count, so an allow discarded by the drain
no longer lets a user-driven block count as consecutive.

fix(web-shell): close the trust-gate and bystander gaps in the local-files bridge (#11169)

* fix(web-shell): close the trust-gate and bystander gaps in the local-files bridge

- Reserve an explicit pending outcome in the workspace route resolver and
  preflight the daemon's client_mcp_over_ws advertisement: while the
  capabilities snapshot has not landed (or the daemon lacks the feature) the
  entry withholds instead of failing open onto the bare /acp primary mount.
- A bystander tab (parked held-elsewhere behind the owner's lock) no longer
  wipes the origin-global grant on disconnect: the record belongs to the
  owner tab, whose bridge keeps running.
- Catch navigator.locks.request rejections in bridge start() (sandboxed
  iframes reject with SecurityError) so the UI reports failed instead of
  parking in connecting with an unhandled rejection.
- Directory skeletons consume the search budget, so a huge near-file-less
  tree cannot hang one tool call; align the design doc's i18n key count and
  fallback description with the implementation.

* fix(web-shell): close the remaining fail-closed edges in the local-files bridge

- Treat an absent `trusted` field like an explicit false in both resolver trust checks (session-context precedent), so a skewed registry payload withholds instead of falling through to the bare primary mount.
- Guard the capabilities feature preflight with an optional chain so a payload without `features` renders the unsupported-daemon blocker instead of throwing during render.
- Reuse fail() in the start() catch so a rejection escaping after connect() opened a socket tears it down instead of leaving it open behind the failed status.
- Extend the zh sweep to the two new blocker states and pin every edge above; the trust and teardown pins are mutation-verified.

* fix(web-shell): close the round-2 review gaps in the local-files bridge

- disconnect() arbitrates the origin-global revoke through the owner lock instead of inferring ownership from a sticky phase: an owned run revokes directly (its own release may still be settling), while a mount that never owned a run clears only when an ifAvailable probe finds the lock free. Fixes both the stale parked tab that reported a successful disconnect over a surviving grant, and the bridge-less phases that wiped a peer tab's live record.
- The browser capability probe now outranks deployment-level withheld reasons at the single injection point, so cross-origin frames keep their recovery affordance on first paint; a withheld entry names the stored grant so the panel's Disconnect (the only revoke path) stays reachable; workspace-resolving gets a transient header and spinner instead of the permanent "Unavailable here".
- Directory skeletons get their own bound and report (truncatedBy directories, dirsScanned in the budget line) so a node_modules-heavy grant can no longer spend the file budget on traversal and answer a definitive "No match"; the unsupported-daemon copy names QWEN_SERVE_CLIENT_MCP_OVER_WS.
- Pins: mutation-verified guards for the arbitration, the owned shortcut, probe precedence, the directory budget, the resolving presentation and the fail() stopped-guard; a positive control for the no-blocker fall-through; a hoisted capabilities override replaces the leaking per-case doMock; one shared exclusive-lock fake for all two-tab cases.
- Deferred, recorded in the PR thread: the held-elsewhere takeover exit (second half of #10962 Finding E).

* fix(web-shell): close the round-3 arbitration and revoke-affordance gaps

- The ownership latch now has the lifetime of the run, not the mount: stopBridge() and the terminal onState phases clear it, and disconnect() reads it before stopping, so a mount whose run already released the lock can no longer skip arbitration and wipe the record a peer tab's live bridge depends on.
- disconnect()'s revoke no longer lets a connect it already invalidated veto the clear (connects are generation-stamped), and the lock arbitration now guards the spec-conformant null decline (Web Locks 4.1) with the same bounded retry start() uses, sharing its attempt/delay constants.
- Withheld entries keep naming the stored grant across the rebind, startBridge and connect status writes, so the panel's Disconnect - the only store.clear() caller - stays reachable over a persisted handle.
- The directory walk bound is driven by limits alone (the dead per-call maxDirs option is gone) with a truthful rationale; the resolver JSDoc no longer over-promises eligibility; the zh matrix pins the transient status line; panel cases pin the revoke affordance under withheld blockers; the wiring positive control asserts selector forwarding.
- Ten new or reworked pins; every guard above is mutation-verified.

* fix(web-shell): make the disconnect revoke outcome-authoritative and share the lock wait

- The revoke veto is decided by the connect generation stamp alone: an in-flight connect receives the deferred revoke through its finally (run when it leaves without saving, dropped when it saves), and a finished connect is decided by whether it saved - closing both the over-clear on a connect that writes during the arbitration window and the under-clear on a cancelled connect that swallowed the revoke.
- disconnect() now reconciles its optimistic terminal status against what the revoke actually achieved (every attempt declined, a soft-failed delete, or a cancelled wait), restoring the parked bridge state or the named grant over idle so the panel never reports a revoke that did not happen.
- connect()'s picker-failure and picker-unavailable writes name the record-backed grant, so a failed pick cannot hide the only revoke affordance over a persisted handle.
- withOwnerLock in bridge-client owns the bounded ifAvailable wait (null-decline guard plus retry) for both start() and the disconnect arbitration; the now-dead DEFAULTS lock fields are gone.
- Pins: a settling-only decline discriminator with recorded attempt causes, save-during-window and cancelled-during-window cases, declined-attempts and soft-failed-delete reconciliation, the picker-failure carry, and the owner-side budget latch; every guard mutation-verified.

* fix(web-shell): keep the deferred local-files revoke arbitrated and the disconnect status truthful (#11169)

The disconnect arbitration could still lose or misreport a user's
revoke on seven measured paths:

- the revoke deferred to a connect's finally ran as a bare store.clear()
  after withOwnerLock had released the lock, wiping a grant a peer had
  since taken over — defer the whole arbitrated unit instead;
- the deferred revoke's boolean outcome was dropped, so a soft-failed
  delete left the panel on the optimistic idle (revoke affordance gone)
  and a successful delete kept naming the cleared grant — reconcile both
  directions inside the parked closure;
- a picker-arm save that failed soft still stamped connectSavedRef,
  vetoing the pending revoke over a record the connect never wrote —
  stamp save()'s boolean (the stored-handle arm keeps its blanket stamp:
  there the record provably holds the same grant);
- the reconcile was not idempotent (parked fact read only from the
  stopped bridge) and fired over a post-disconnect connect's own status
  and over a live withheld blocker — read the rendered status too, gate
  on the connect generation, and restore the pre-click blocker;
- the arbitration's cancellation epoch was bumped by unmount, silently
  cancelling the user's revoke inside the inter-attempt backoff — use a
  disconnect-only epoch for cancellation and the revoke guard.

Each guard is pinned by a focused witness test that is red under its
mutation probe and against the pre-round source.

window. A rebind that keeps serving the in-memory handle over a foreign
record re-asserts the latch startBridge clears, and a soft-failed re-save
never disarms it.

* fix(web-shell): guard the ownWrite record read against a missing store

tsconfig.lib.json (the CI build gate) flags what the package typecheck
missed: with no store, revoke()'s load() resolves undefined and the
ownWrite computation dereferenced it before the undefined guard below.

* fix(web-shell): decide record ownership by entry identity in revoke

R13: revoke() — the only production store.clear() caller — still certified
the origin-global record by basename, so a same-basename peer overwrite in
steady state (no blip, no session switch) was deleted by Disconnect, and the
ownWrite exclusion actively skipped the guard for connect-bound grants. The
foreign latch also outlived proofs that should clear it (identity-proven
re-bind, forced rebuild over a soft-failed save), parked restore/connect/
rebind continuations wrote across disconnects and fresh binds, and restore()'s
blocker arm replaced the panel's truthful bound name with the record's.

Key revoke()'s veto, ownWrite and foreign decisions on isSameEntry against
stamped handle objects (fail-closed on rejection, name kept only as the
no-handle fallback); give the rebind continuation an epoch every bridge build
bumps; re-check the generation after every new identity await; let the rebind
effect own the latch reset over the in-memory grant; name the stored record
only when the panel has no name of its own.

* fix(web-shell): close the parked-continuation and latch-reset gaps

R14: restore()'s identity re-check sat inside the true arm, so a disconnect
landing in the identity await fell through to boundLiveMatch/startBridge and
rebuilt the bridge over a peer record behind the click; restore() also never
invalidated its parked load against a concurrent connect save; the rebind
effect wrote the foreign latch one-way at the decision point, dropping
entry-identity proofs on the exits that never reach startBridge (permission
lapsed), which left a stale latch over the user's own record; and the deferred
revoke closure treated "a connect is still in flight" as proof it had
re-deferred, though a declined re-arbitration never runs revoke() and parks
nothing, leaving the panel without its only revoke button.

Hoist the restore re-check above both exits and fold a save epoch (bumped at
both connect save sites) into every post-await gate; assign the latch
two-way at the rebind decision point; key the deferred closure's guard on the
re-deferral actually having happened.

* fix(web-shell): close the round-15 revoke-evidence and epoch gaps

- restore(): stop folding the live detach latch into staleRestore() — the
  explicit detached naming branch below it was unreachable, so a declined
  disconnect left the panel without the record's name and its only revoke
  affordance; the detach check stays on the post-identity re-check.
- startBridge(): bump the handle epoch at the bind (below the live-bridge
  exemption), not at the build, so a needs-session bind still invalidates
  a parked rebind continuation.
- rebind: fold the connect save epoch into staleRebind() so a committed
  same-entry re-save (which builds nothing) supersedes a parked record
  load instead of being re-latched foreign.
- disconnect(): gate the bridgeHandleRef fallback on a live bridge (the
  stamp outlives its bridge and would condemn the next named record), and
  decide record ownership against namedRecordRef — the handle stashed by
  every naming write — refusing to clear when no ownership evidence exists
  instead of comparing the record's name against the name read from it.

* fix(web-shell): let identity retire the latch and keep live withholds

R15: revoke() ORed the stale foreign latch with the fresh entry-identity
proof, so a record a peer swapped back while no effect re-ran could never be
released and the panel lost its only clearing button; restore()'s
permission-lapsed exit wrote needs-gesture over a live, correctly-routed
bridge (hiding Disconnect over registered tools) and erased a withhold that
landed while it was parked; connect()'s re-armed-gesture and picker-failed
exits hardcoded blocker:null and clobbered withholds that landed mid-prompt
or mid-picker.

Retire the latch on a fresh identity proof (fail-closed on rejecting
isSameEntry, never on a name match); read boundLiveMatch() and the live
blocker mirror before the needs-gesture write; read the live mirror in both
connect exits so a live withhold keeps its phase and its copy.

* fix(web-shell): stop released grants from re-arming delete authority

R16: after this mount's revoke cleared the record, nothing reset the display
stash or the detach premise, so effect-driven naming writes adopted a record
a peer wrote afterwards and revoke() accepted it as ownership evidence —
deleting the peer's persisted grant. Gate the four effect-driven naming
writes on a releasedRecordRef set when a clear actually succeeds (cleared
where detachedRef is), and drop the stale stash on success so a peer's
re-grant of the same entry cannot self-certify.

R16 also: the owned latch skipped all arbitration while a peer could already
hold the lock this disconnect freed. Await the run's lock release becoming
visible (bounded by one retry delay), then probe: free means no peer depends
on the record; a decline can only mean a peer holds it, so the revoke
arbitrates instead of deleting out from under the peer's bridge.

* fix(web-shell): hold the owner lock across the owner-side delete

R17: the release-visibility probe released the lock before revoke() ran its
read-decide-delete, so a peer waking from its retry budget inside revoke's
awaits still bridged a record being deleted. Run revoke() inside the probe
callback so the lock is held across the delete; a declined probe still falls
through to withOwnerLock, and the not-visible fast path stays unarbitrated.

R18: the deferred revoke's reconcile read connectWroteStatusRef after its own
arbitration await, so a connect started inside that window reset the flag and
the reconcile overwrote the handing-off connect's authoritative status.
Snapshot the flag at the closure's entry, before the first await.

fix(models): refresh expired provider inventory in background (#146317)

## What Problem This Solves

New provider models stay hidden after saved inventory expires, until an explicit refresh.

## Why This Change Was Made

#136915 removed repeat acquisition when it reused prepared catalogs. This restores expiry-driven discovery without making readers wait. @steipete for awareness.

Production +199/-105 (net +94); test tooling +7/-4; tests/support +214/-6; docs +5. Growth carries original cache deadlines through the existing acquisition path; duplicate normalization and separate inventory maps are removed.

## User Impact

Reads return saved rows immediately, then show new models after renewal. Failed providers keep saved rows and their warning while healthy siblings renew.

## Evidence

Telegram/Gateway with synthetic responses: main kept 8 rows after expiry; saved rows returned in 90 ms, then the ninth appeared. CLI agrees. Post-login reply: 67 ms. 16 valid config shapes started; invalid legacy input rejected. Getter-backed results retain accepted rows. Full consumer details: `consumers.md`.

## Compatibility

No config keys, database changes, migrations, or public plugin API changes.

## Consumers

- `models.list`, CLI, selectors, `/models`, `/think` menus, and sticker vision: renewed metadata.
- Public agent-runtime getters and setup-shell thinking defaults: saved metadata can start background renewal.
- `models status`: renewed metadata for visibility.
- Chat metadata publication listener: invalidates cached metadata after renewal.
- Catalog warnings: persist until the failed scope succeeds or its inputs change. CLI row output omits the warning.

census: generic refreshCommittedProviderCatalogs reviewed — 2 callers listed
census: generic error reviewed — 0 callers listed

## Invalidation

Cache hits and compatible reloads preserve deadlines. Changed credentials, provider settings, or plugins retire old facts. Restart rebuilds inventory. Explicit refresh retries failures; native refresh retains its scope.

## Contention

Existing discovery queue and pending request; concurrent reads return saved rows during a held response.

## Tests

Registered `models.list`: expiry, accepted projection, held responses, coalescing, failed siblings, warning recovery. Reload-auth cases: startup/reload publication and snapshot access. Startup-static and test-harness edits produce reply fixtures. Owner/cache checks pass; the test runner prepares the SDK runtime first. Structural checks pass.

Co-authored-by: Ayaan Zaidi <hi@obviy.us>

fix(agents): forward ordered saved subscription credentials to CLI runs (#146095)

## What Problem This Solves

A saved subscription token was dropped before CLI execution unless the account was explicitly selected. Default turns reported “Not logged in” and used the configured fallback (#144793).

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared selector forwards saved subscription credentials using account order. This restores 2026.9.1 behavior and reverses the forwarding restriction from #144266. @MasterSwords1 for awareness.

## User Impact

New sessions use saved subscription tokens without an account selection or native login file. Existing sessions keep their account and history until the user selects another account or the stored profile is removed.

## Evidence

- Token-only default: before, all 10 turns failed at 1/2/3/4 concurrency; after, all succeeded without fallback.
- Native conversation: before, saving a token and restarting switched accounts and omitted history; after, the real CLI resumed the same native session with prior history. Fresh sessions and explicit changes used the saved token.
- Registered `chat.send` → `agent.wait` → `chat.history` and recording endpoints exercised both paths. All 16 valid saved-config fixtures reached readiness; the invalid legacy fixture was rejected. Published 2026.9.1 passed the token-only cases.

## Compatibility

Explicit pins, native selections and empty orders retain their meaning. Provider API keys require explicit selection for this subscription route. Cross-account history protection and fallback policy are unchanged. No schema, config-key or API changes.

## Consumers

- Chat replies and scheduled turns: keep the session account.
- Direct CLI turns: preserve scoped credentials for every supported backend.
- System-agent setup: uses the ordered saved credential; verified conversations retain their bound route.
- Integration-test scheduling: prepares runtime artifacts using existing runner capacity.

## Invalidation

Each turn reads current credentials and the session binding; saving tokens or changing account order preserves an existing account, while profile removal or a new session permits selection, and restart restores the saved binding.

## Contention

No new lock or queue. Real CLI overlap at 2/3/4 turns passed; Gateway health responded within 0.8 seconds.

## Tests

Five registered chat cases cover defaults, native continuity, explicit changes, account order/removal, empty order and API-key-only setup. All 152 direct CLI cases pass. Timing and planner baselines are unchanged.

fix(channels): Slack task cards repeat the command text when a command finishes (#143880)

* fix(channels): keep the shown command detail only for a restated command output

A command output event describes its command through the agent's item
title ("command <meta>"). With commandText raw the shared progress line
builder uses that title as the output line's detail, a second description
of the command whose detail the progress line already shows from the tool
start. The compositor's merge kept the shown detail only when the output
line had none, so a finished command line changed its detail from
"run tests" to "command run tests". Slack's native task rows append
details instead of replacing them, so the card read
"run tests · command run tests" and the plan header was relabeled
"Exec — command run tests"; channels that render the draft as text showed
the relabeled command.

The merge now keeps the detail the reader has been watching when the
output line's detail is a restatement of it: empty, the line's own status,
the shown detail itself, or the shown detail behind a "command" prefix
(whitespace collapsed, prefix case-insensitive). Any other incoming detail
replaces the shown one as before, so a command-output line that ever
carries real output or a different description is not discarded. A line
that already ended (a failed nested command, the Matrix recovery case) is
still replaced whole when the output names no command, so a recovered run
does not keep stale failure text, and an output line arriving for a line
that showed no detail keeps its own.

The embedded exec producer ends its command item before the command
output arrives: tool start, tool and command items opening as running, a
status-only output projected from the tool result, the tool and command
items ending as completed or failed, then the command_output event titled
"command <meta>". The terminal item made the shown line terminal, so the
restated output replaced it whole and relabeled the command after all.
The ended-line rule therefore applies only when the output carries no
command of its own; an output that names the shown command keeps the
shown detail through the terminal item. streaming.command-item.test.ts
walks that full sequence for a failed and a completed command and keeps
the recovery case.

The Telegram progress preview test now expects the finished line to read
"exit 2; false", the command text the tool line showed, rather than
"exit 2; command false"; its purpose, keeping command output out of the
preview, is unchanged.

The two lifecycle tests that check the output line is used as is compare
the merged line to the output line structurally, with the id left open,
rather than by object identity, so this change stacks in either order
with the companion fix that keeps a merged line's original id and returns
a copy of the line. The Slack tests live in a new
progress-blocks.command-output.test.ts because progress-blocks.test.ts is
at the max-lines limit; the optional third reconcile batch is read as
possibly undefined under the extension typecheck's strict index access.

A new Telegram loopback test, bot-message-dispatch.progress-command-detail
.telegram-http.test.ts, drives the real dispatchTelegramMessage through the
shared dispatcher, the Telegram progress compositor, the draft stream, and
grammY against a loopback Bot API server, with only the reply resolver
synthetic. It records the sendMessage/editMessageText payloads for the
unit fixture's two-event sequence and for the embedded producer's full
sequence, and expects the progress message to be sent as "Exec false" and
edited in place to "Exec false exit 2"; before this change the same edit
read "Exec command false exit 2". The Telegram dispatch unit test gains
the same embedded sequence.

fix(backup): preserve cyclic symbolic links during archive creation (#146161)

## What Problem This Solves

A state directory containing `loop-a -> loop-b -> loop-a` makes `openclaw backup create --verify --json` fail with `Private update capture marker is unreadable; export refused.` No archive is created.

## Why This Change Was Made

The decision `whether a selected path is a private update-capture location` is made by exactly one mechanism at `src/infra/update-capture-paths.ts:151`. It resolves links component by component with `lstat`, cycle detection, and a depth limit, retains each selected entry name for legacy capture ownership, and checks real selected and resolved directories for privacy markers. The separate canonical scan is removed.

Resolved marked targets remain excluded. Linked directory owners and capture-root aliases still protect legacy capture contents. SQLite snapshots use the same assertion before copying selected contents. The separate update-time backup work in #144005 writes privacy markers and uses this classifier.

## User Impact

Cyclic and dangling links no longer prevent backup creation. Their original link text is preserved. Marked targets and private capture contents stay out of archives, while ordinary unmarked links retain the behavior from #141925.

## Evidence

- Pinned main `c1a39f89`: real CLI exits 1 with the reported error and no archive. Head `6c58557e`: cycle/dangling creation, verification, and restoration succeed with exact links and payload.
- The marked-target archive omits the link and private bytes, then verifies and restores on v2026.9.4. A linked sibling owner also excludes legacy capture contents. Malformed and unreadable real markers refuse without publishing an archive.
- Head `057dbc07`: config selected through a private capture-root alias refuses export with no archive. A containing-workspace archive omits the alias and private bytes, then verifies and restores on both current code and v2026.9.4 with healthy bytes intact.
- All 199 targeted tests passed, including component ordering, repeated links, trailing separators, archive privacy, and support exports. Complete dispositions and compatibility details are retained in `consumers.md`.

## Compatibility

The archive format is unchanged. Capture-root alias and marked-target archives restore on v2026.9.4 with zero links and exact healthy bytes. Plain and portable relative-link archives retain their passing compatibility checks.

Only cyclic/dangling-link output receives the additional old-reader allowance. v2026.9.4 cannot restore preserved cycles and reports `Backup restore failed; the incomplete target was cleaned: <restore-target>`; the updated reader restores them. Existing restrictions on ordinary absolute links predate this fix. No shim is added. Focused CLI proof runs on macOS; Windows junction coverage depends on CI.

## Consumers

- Backup inventory and archive creation preserve unresolved links while excluding resolved private targets and real private ancestors.
- Legacy capture exclusion recognizes sibling owners and capture roots reached through directory links.
- SQLite archive snapshots apply the same content admission before capture or reuse.

## Invalidation

None. Each call inspects current filesystem metadata; no cached classification or persistent state changes.

## Contention

No lock, queue, transaction, or asynchronous publication changes.

## Tests

`backupCreateCommand` and `backupRestoreCommand` cover marked-target omission, linked-owner exclusion, capture-root alias refusal, loop/dangling preservation, and restored bytes. Real and resolved marker refusals remain covered. The canonical database alias test retains refusal of an incomplete hardlink inventory and the unmarked sanitation control. No tests were deleted.

**Follow-ups:** Add command-level coverage for path-resolution edge cases and test path separators on native Windows.

fix(ui): publish initial model catalog on connect (#145927)

## What Problem This Solves

The first web model picker open could wait seven seconds for a catalog reply. A late initial snapshot could also restore an old saved account after the user changed it.

## Why This Change Was Made

Publish the existing catalog during connection setup through the authenticated request dispatcher. Initial and ordinary replies use the same cache publication checks, so delayed work cannot replace a newer session selection.

## User Impact

Published choices appear on first open and reconnect while discovery continues. Warm reopen stays fast, without an extra catalog request from opening the picker.

## Evidence

With catalog replies held for seven seconds, the original picker had no usable choices until the reply. The corrected New Session and active-chat pickers showed rows within 100 ms; warm reopen took 8–12 ms. Neither open added a request.

Real browser/Gateway tests cover reconnect and a saved-account change before snapshot completion. Sixteen valid configuration fixtures start; an invalid legacy fixture rejects as expected. Previous-version source builds connect in both directions; installed-release upgrades were not tested. Full consumer analysis: `consumers.md`.

## Compatibility

The new connect field is sent only after server advertisement. Clients without opt-in receive no snapshot. No protocol-version bump, configuration key, database change, or migration.

## Consumers

- New Session picker: uses published rows before its ordinary catalog reply.
- Active-chat picker: receives the saved session's model/account projection and retains newer selections.
- Mounted browser shell: preserves initial publication across reconnect.

## Invalidation

Connection, identity, configuration, session metadata, session mutations, and explicit refresh retire stale reads. Expiry and eviction retain publication ordering; delayed results cannot refill invalidated state.

## Contention

Snapshot publication adds no lock, transaction, or await. The existing dispatcher owns catalog reads; the common cache owner admits results synchronously.

## Tests

Browser picker tests exercise fresh, saved-session, refresh, and reconnect flows. Gateway tests enter connect, `models.list`, and `sessions.patch`. Handshake, cache, metadata, and sibling checks pass. The shared test partition guard passes with the server grouping from #146212. Full automated validation is still required.

fix: adopt Settings write revisions across draft replay (#146002)

Related: #145939. Context: #145983 (server acknowledgement owner; no landing-order dependency).

## What Problem This Solves

A Settings edit reverted during its save can leave the first value on disk and show **Settings changed elsewhere**, without an external writer. Raw edits during autosave, patch acknowledgements and teardown also exposed stale draft revisions. A hashless preference no-op could additionally clear a real form conflict and let a later edit overwrite an external value.

## Why This Change Was Made

The decision `what base revision the client holds after an acknowledged write` is made by exactly one mechanism at `ui/src/lib/config/config-draft-model.ts:431`, `adoptConfigWriteAck`. Set, Apply, patch, independent preference/plugin writes and teardown consume it. Canonical source and base revision advance together before any null-replay return.

Form replay uses owned sanitized objects, including clean reverts; raw-text form replay and separate patch adoption are deleted. Raw buffers keep exact bytes and their original content evidence until canonical changes are incorporated.

The shared input requires `independentSnapshot`. Loaded independent writes supply their pre-write source; no-ops supply the source admitted by the existing versioned read owner. Full-draft writes explicitly supply null; null also represents an independent write before initial load. A no-op read cannot count as a committed form submission.

The draft owner compares both orders of form replay, using the existing redaction projection. Disjoint or matching edits agree; divergent overlapping edits retain original content and conflict before originals are replaced. Raw-document validation stays strict. No new caller guard, read owner, generation check or adoption branch is added. The extra content validation and two typed existing-writer adapters account for production growth.

## User Impact

Reverts and raw edits use the acknowledged revision. Form replay preserves compatible canonical changes; stale raw content and conflicting form values remain protected. Apply and retained-client teardown use the same continuation owner. Reconnect-paused drafts still require explicit submission.

Actual app shutdown stops the Gateway before capability disposal; teardown proof is at the registered capability boundary. No server response, config key, protocol, schema, SDK, migration, updater, native or CLI behavior changes.

Revert uses the old revision, receives INVALID_REQUEST and leaves logging debug on disk. Candidate blocked/normal-parser runs persist info with visible **Saved**.
- Retained browser proof covers raw edits during form autosave, stale raw rejection/recovery, ordinary autosave, concurrent external edits and navigation. Exact patch-in-flight form continuation uses its receipt hash with every later config read held and displays **Saved**.
- On `0a67e190`, a real preference no-op clears a retained form conflict; an unrelated console edit then saves stale logging debug over external error and displays Saved. The corrected registered regression preserves the conflict, original content and external value.
- On committed `66df3f9`, the same real no-op preserves the conflict; another form edit sends no unsafe write and the external value stays on disk. Visible Reload followed by a safe edit displays **Saved** and preserves that value. Complete red/green order, files and sanitized captures are retained.

Formatting, focused lint, line-limit, assertion and all three unused-export scans pass. Type checking and full CI remain hosted.

## Invalidation

Every acknowledged write advances the canonical snapshot and draft base together. Original form evidence advances only after compatible replay; incompatible external overlaps retain that evidence and conflict. Raw originals retain their content anchor until the full document incorporates canonical changes. Editing, mode switches, discard and parser generation retain their existing lifecycles.

Only real write receipts invalidate older reads. Hashless no-ops follow the existing versioned read/successor/connection owner and supply its admitted source for content compatibility; reading a new revision does not authorize a stale form overwrite. Disconnect and reconnect retire flights; only unacknowledged full-draft bytes support lost-ack inference. Disposal retains receipt adoption while existing dispatch admission remains enforced.

## Contention

The existing single writer serializes writes and no-op source reconciliation. The corrected-head disjoint contention case queued a registered save for 14,763 ms with zero premature sets, while visible Logs navigation and eight reads completed. Four milliseconds after release, the save used the newer admitted revision, preserved both values and settled saved. Settings controls were disabled during reads, so the competing write is explicitly capability-level proof. The Logs page did not display Saved. This affected no-op case was rerun for this correction; unaffected concurrent external-edit proof is retained.

fix(reef): park capacity-failed inbound delivery instead of unwinding the shared inbox (#144637)

* fix(reef): park capacity-failed inbound delivery instead of unwinding the shared inbox

Bounded Reef delivered-marker and replay stores fail closed on capacity
(reject-new), but those failures surfaced as ordinary inbox errors: the
shared connection treated them as transport failures, tore down, and
retried from the unchanged cursor, head-of-line blocking every other
peer's entries and re-entering inbound handling without a durable
outcome.

- Reserve the delivered marker before ingress and confirm after, so a
  verified entry has a durable retry-safe outcome before inbound
  handling and retried entries classify by marker state instead of
  re-entering ingress.
- Classify store-capacity errors as parked inbox outcomes (retry-safe,
  no teardown, other peers keep flowing) instead of raw failures.
- Legacy stateless delivered markers (doctor import, earlier releases)
  read as delivered; no migration or config change.

* test(reef): satisfy assertion-safety ratchet and await-thenable lint

Mark new test transport/replay stubs and the plugin-state capacity probe
with SAFETY comments, and drop an await of the sync keyed store's
registerIfAbsent in the legacy-marker test.

* test(reef): prove capacity-parked delivery through the production inbox connection

Drive ReefInboxConnection -> ReefMessageFlow -> SQLite delivered/replay
stores with only the relay and platform send mocked: two peers' entries
park independently without unwinding the shared inbox while later
entries stay attemptable, both complete once capacity frees with a
persisted cursor past them, an interrupted reservation re-ingresses
exactly once and confirms on restart, and a legacy stateless marker
suppresses re-ingress with an ack-only redelivery.

* fix(reef): keep reservations out of the delivered namespace for older readers

Review found that a pending reservation stored in the delivered namespace
would be treated as a completed delivery by older Reef readers, so a
rollback could acknowledge never-delivered messages.

- Move reservations to a separate delivered-pending namespace; the
  delivered namespace keeps its exact historical record shape, so older
  readers are rollback-safe and can never mistake a reservation for a
  delivery.
- Confirm writes the delivered marker and clears the reservation;
  interrupted deliveries keep the reservation pending and re-ingress on
  the next poll.
- Classify confirm-time capacity failures as parked outcomes too, so a
  full delivered store parks the entry after ingress instead of
  unwinding the shared inbox.
- Regression coverage: reservation visibility to has(), per-namespace
  capacity failures for reserve and confirm, post-ingress park with a
  pending reservation, and the production-path recovery proof updated.

* test(reef): drive recovery proof over SQLite replay stores and a true restart

The capacity-recovery connection tests now run the production SQLite
replay store, and the interrupted-delivery case restarts with freshly
opened store handles over the same persisted state directory, matching
the upgrade/restart coverage the review asked for.

* fix(reef): keep the reservation namespace constant internal

The pending-namespace constant has no production consumers outside its
module; un-export it and reference the namespace value literally in the
recovery test to satisfy the deadcode export gate.

* fix(reef): make reservation confirmation capacity-neutral

Review found that inserting the delivered marker before deleting the
reservation could hit the plugin-wide aggregate row limit: the
reservation consumed the last live row and blocked its own confirmation
after ingress had already run.

Confirmation now frees the reservation row first, so the transition
never needs two live rows at once; a crash between the steps leaves
neither record and the re-poll re-ingresses at-least-once. Cover the
plugin-wide aggregate limit with a squeezed-limit regression test and
update the post-ingress park test for the clean-retry behavior.

* reef: keep delivery reservations process-local

Persisted two-phase markers duplicated the store's own at-least-once
semantics and added a cross-restart contract the maintainer has not
signed off on. In-flight reservations now live in a process-local set:
they classify entries within a single run, never consume store
capacity, and the persisted delivered markers plus replay store carry
the shipped durability contract unchanged. A crash in the
dispatch-confirm window re-dispatches once on restart — the same
bounded behavior the shipped store already exhibits.

Removes the delivered-pending namespace; reserve-full capacity parking
(no longer reachable) and rollback-safe reserve guard retained.
