repos.description: 🚀 The easiest way to automate building and releasing your iOS and Android apps

commits.message:
[ci] run full workflows on master as they stack (#30218)

* chore: run full workflows on main as they stack

* chore: queue master for all builds
[ci] chore: treat 'both' as 'all' for all 3 platforms (#30214)

[tests] Give each spec its own scratch directory instead of /tmp/fastlane (#30217)

Seven action specs used `/tmp/fastlane/tests/fastlane` as a scratch directory
and one used `/tmp/fastlane/template.html`. The path is machine-global, so
every rspec process `rake test_parallel` starts shares it, and several specs
delete it while others are using it.

`update_app_identifier_spec` is the sharpest case: its `after` hook removes
the whole `tests/fastlane` tree, once per example, and six other spec files
write their fixtures there. A worker running it deletes what another worker's
`before` hook has just written, and that worker fails on a file it created
itself microseconds earlier.

Running the two spec files against each other in two rspec processes, the
victim failed 3 times in 15 runs before this change and 0 times after:

    1) ... throws an error when the entitlements file does not exist
       Failure/Error: File.delete(File.join(test_path, entitlements_path))
       Errno::ENOENT:

The same race reached CI as a different symptom, the action reporting
"Could not find entitlements file" where the spec expected "cannot be parsed".

Each spec now takes a `Dir.mktmpdir` of its own and removes it afterwards, so
nothing is shared and no spec can reach another's fixtures. The explicit
`mkdir_p` calls go away because `mktmpdir` creates the directory, and the
per-file cleanup becomes one `remove_entry` of the whole tree, which also
stops `update_plist_spec` leaking the `bundle.xcodeproj` copy it never
deleted.

`private_public_fastfile_spec` also wiped `/tmp/fastlane` on every example
even though `FastfilePrivatePublic` writes nothing at all, so that line is
pure collateral damage on other workers and is removed.

This does not cover `fast_file_spec` and the fixture Fastfiles, which share
`/tmp/fastlane` itself rather than the `tests/fastlane` subtree; they need the
fixtures to learn the path and are left to a follow-up.

See fastlane#30184.

test: stop a spec mutating the plist fixture another spec reads (#30215)

set_info_plist_value_spec saved, mutated, asserted and restored ./fastlane/spec/fixtures/plist/Info.plist, a tracked fixture. The checkout is shared by every worker when the suite is split, so get_info_plist_value_spec on another worker could read the window in between and get NewValue<timestamp> where it expected com.krausefx.app. That is what failed on Windows in CI.

The window is small, which is why it is rare and why it does not reproduce by running the two files against each other a few times. Polling the fixture while the writer runs measures it: 2 hits in 4000 polls without this change, 0 with it.

Work on a copy in a temporary directory instead. That removes the restore step as well as the race, since nothing else can observe the file. The output file moves to its own temporary directory too, rather than the shared /tmp/fastlane/tests tree.

Same shape as the clipboard race in fastlane#30210: a spec doing save, mutate, assert, restore on a resource it does not own.

[spaceship] Read the App Store Connect API key from where Apple keeps it now (#30206)

* [spaceship] read the API key from where App Store Connect keeps it now

Apple removed the olympus endpoint this key came from, so every Apple ID login fails. Its own front end no longer fetches the key either, it carries it, and the sign out route hands it out in a redirect:

  HEAD /logout -> 302 Location: .../appleauth/signout?widgetKey=<key>&asop=destroy-session

Read it from there, and keep the olympus call as a fallback in case it returns, since that is the source Apple documented rather than one read out of a redirect. Failing to read the redirect returns nil rather than raising, so the fallback is reached instead of this becoming a new single point of failure.

Two things about that request are load bearing rather than incidental.

It sends no cookies. The redirect points at a signout with asop=destroy-session, so asking for it over the connection that carries the session jar would end the session this method is called in order to establish. The connection is built bare for that reason, and a spec asserts the middleware stack has neither a cookie jar nor redirect following, because a comment saying so would not survive someone reusing the client's own connection.

It does not follow the redirect. The key is in the Location header; following it is what performs the signout.

A hardcoded key was considered and rejected. Apple has already rotated this one, and a stale constant does not fail closed: it gets through the key step and through SIRP and 2FA, then the session is refused later with a 401 that points nowhere near the cause. Reading the current value is both more robust and a better failure when it is wrong.

Reported and diagnosed in fastlane#30199.

* [spaceship] do not swallow a local error while reading the sign out redirect

The rescue around the sign out fetch caught StandardError so that anything unexpected falls through to the other source. That put back the problem fastlane#30198 is about: a local failure, a missing log directory being the one that started that issue, would be swallowed here and the caller handed whatever the fallback had to say about itself instead of the real cause.

Narrow it to what the request can be expected to go wrong with, Faraday errors and an unparseable Location. Anything else is a bug or a local problem and is worth seeing.

* test: stub the sign out request the API key now comes from

Nine of nine CI jobs failed on the previous commit while the suite passed locally, because a cached key left in the temporary directory by an earlier run short circuits itc_service_key before it reaches the network. With no cache, which is every clean checkout, the new request runs and WebMock blocks it.

Stub it for every spaceship example rather than only the ones that log in: the key is fetched by whichever request first needs it, so an unstubbed one passes on a machine that has run the suite before and fails on a clean one, which is the failure this is.

* [spaceship] warn when the sign out redirect cannot be read

Review feedback on #30206. This was logging at debug, which is wrong for what it means: the sign out redirect is where the key normally comes from, so failing there means the run is about to depend on the olympus endpoint that Apple has already removed once.

If that fallback fails too, its message is all the caller sees. This line is the half that explains why the fallback was reached at all, and at debug nobody has it.

Also matches the two cache failures a few lines up, which already warn for the same kind of thing: a best effort step did not work and the run carried on. The success path stays at debug.

[tests] Stop two spec files racing for the system clipboard (#30211)

* test: stop two spec files racing for the system clipboard

Three files drove the real pasteboard, each saving it, writing to it, asserting on it and restoring it. Split across processes, any two of them overlapping fight over a resource there is only one of per machine:

  expected: ""
       got: "Some value: 1789198149"

That value is written by fastlane's clipboard action spec, in another gem, on another worker. The spaceauth example had saved an empty pasteboard and asserted after the other worker overwrote it.

This one has no isolation lever. ENV and the working directory are per process, HOME and TMPDIR can be redirected, and none of that helps: there is one pasteboard per session and every process shares it. It cannot be fixed by ordering either, because it is a genuine race rather than a dependency on what ran first.

Only one of the three is about the pasteboard. The other two use it as a convenient observable, so they now assert against the helper instead: spaceauth cares whether the runner copied the session, and the action spec cares that the action passes its value through. fastlane_core's own clipboard spec keeps driving pbcopy and pbpaste, which is what it exists to test, and is now the only thing touching them.

Fixes fastlane#30210.

* docs: say that this is the only unmocked clipboard test, and why

The suite keeps exactly one test using the real pasteboard, and the reason is not obvious from the file. There is one pasteboard per logged-in session, shared by every process, so a second spec touching it on another worker races for it. Everywhere else it is mocked, which is what lets the suite run split.

This one stays unmocked because it is the test of the pbcopy and pbpaste boundary itself. Keeping exactly one means there is nothing for it to race with.

Also records the cost, which is real: it modifies the user's environment while it runs. It saves the pasteboard and puts it back, but anything copied in that window is lost.

[spaceship] say what actually went wrong fetching the API key (#30205)

itc_service_key wrapped its whole body in a bare rescue and re-raised everything as AppleTimeoutError with "this might be a server issue", so the message named neither the failure nor its cause.

Apple's key endpoint now returns 404, which makes this concrete. The 404 body is an HTML error page rather than JSON, and String#[] on it returns nil for the key being looked up, so the code raised "Service key is empty" and the user was told about a server timeout. Neither says what happened.

Check the status and report it. A 5xx stays an AppleTimeoutError, since that is worth retrying and with_retry decides from the class. A 4xx becomes an UnexpectedResponse, which is not retried: a permanent failure previously cost five attempts and four three second sleeps before failing anyway.

A 2xx response without the key now says so rather than borrowing the empty key message.

Reading and writing the local cache are best effort. Having the key and failing to save it is not a reason to fail the login, and an unreadable cache is a reason to fetch the key again rather than to stop. Both log instead of raising, which is what fastlane#30198 asked for.

Only a genuine timeout or connection failure still raises AppleTimeoutError, which is the one case the old message was right about.

Reported in fastlane#30199.

[core] stop hardcoding /tmp where a real path is needed (#30209)

"/tmp" is not a directory on every platform Ruby runs on. On Windows it resolves against the current drive, so a write to it raises Errno::ENOENT unless something else happens to have created D:\tmp first, and a chdir into it fails outright.

Every remaining place that uses it as a real path rather than as an example now asks for Dir.tmpdir:

- itunes_transporter, thirteen default parameters plus the download destination, which is the one that chdirs
- deliver, the parent directory the upload package is staged in, four callers
- spaceship, the copy made to strip the alpha channel from a screenshot
- lcov, the intermediate coverage file
- build_and_upload_to_appetize, its staging directory
- update_project_provisioning, the default location the WWDR certificate is downloaded to

On macOS this also moves these out of the shared /tmp and into the per user directory, so a file written by one user no longer blocks another. On Linux Dir.tmpdir is /tmp unless TMPDIR says otherwise, so nothing changes there.

What is left is documentation: the example snippets in scp, rsync, erb and spaceship_logs, where the path is illustrative and in two cases is a remote one, and two Helper.test? fixtures in hg_commit_version_bump that are string arithmetic rather than filesystem access.

Originally reviewed and approved as #30204, which was merged into a base branch that had already been squashed into master, so its changes never reached master. Recreated here on top of master unchanged.

Run the CI suite as several processes (#30202)

* ci: run the suite as several processes on every platform

The CI matrix ran `rake test_all`, one rspec process per job, which is where most of the nine minutes went. `rake test_parallel` runs the same suite split across workers. Same nine configurations, same Ruby and Xcode versions, same platforms.

Four workers rather than the task's own min(cores, 8), which is three on the macOS runners. Each worker spends much of its time waiting on an xcodebuild child rather than holding a core, and four measured best on both runner shapes.

The json the report action reads is assembled by the rake task, which joins what the workers each wrote.

* ci: keep the worker logs when a matrix job fails

A worker writes its rspec output to its own log rather than to stdout, so a failing job listed which examples failed and never why. Upload them, as the split workflow already does.

* docs: say what the split workflow is for now that CI runs the split

The speed argument moved to the CI workflow, which runs `rake test_parallel` on every pull request. What is left here is the two things that workflow does not do: keeping the per platform timings current, and running the split in a random order rather than the defined one.

Renamed to match, since "Parallel tests" now describes the CI workflow rather than this one.

Run the spec suite as several processes (#30191)

* test: run the spec suite as several processes, and record what to balance from

The suite takes about 562s on a macOS runner. Split across four workers
it takes about 150s, and across twelve on a developer machine it goes
from 276s to 41s.

  rake test_parallel              split across min(cores, 12) workers
  WORKERS=4 rake test_parallel
  rake spec_timings               record per file durations to balance from
  rake test_tune                  sweep worker counts and say which is fastest

Balanced on recorded durations rather than file size, which is a poor
stand in: one xcodebuild example outweighs a thousand pure ones, and
weighting by size put 4006 examples in one worker against 1195 in
another. Four workers went from 2.2x to 3.68x on the same machine from
the balancing alone.

Timings are per platform, in internal/spec_timings.<platform>.json, and
none are committed here: they are recorded by CI, on the runner they
describe, and committed separately. A file also records where it was
measured, the date, the core count, the Ruby and the Xcode, because a
split is only as good as its numbers and numbers from a 14 core laptop
describe a 3 core runner badly. Without a file the split falls back to
weighting by file size and says so.

Per platform because the suite is a different shape on each. 61% of the example time
on macOS is in requires_xcodebuild files, and those skip entirely on
Linux: three of the heaviest macOS files cost nothing there. Balancing a
Linux split from macOS numbers left a worker idle 41% to 48% of the run
against 12% with its own numbers, and took the wall clock from 58-70s to
43s.

Files heavier than one worker's share are cut into runs of examples,
addressed with rspec's own path[id,id] syntax. Without that the slowest
single file is a floor no number of workers gets under: at 269s of
example time and a 35s worst file, seven workers was the most that could
help.

Each worker reports the time rspec measured, and the run reports the
spread between fastest and slowest and how much worker time was spent
waiting for the straggler. The wall clock is the slowest worker plus
start up, so a split is only as good as its worst bucket, and the
prediction printed beforehand comes from timings recorded elsewhere.

Processes rather than threads: ENV and the working directory are per
process in the kernel, so a worker cannot corrupt another through
either. Threads would overlap the subprocess waits, measured at 3.96x
against 1.01x for CPU bound work, but Dir.chdir is process wide and
refuses concurrent use, and RSpec is not thread safe.

* ci: run the split on its own pull requests, and everything quarterly

Two jobs split the suite across workers on macOS and Linux, with
--order random so that each worker shuffles its own subset. That covers
both axes at once: which files run together, and in what order. They are
different tests. A split puts a spec in a context no seed produces, and
that is how the DisplayType global and the pty exit status defect
(#30188) were found, neither of which a random order had turned up.

Two more jobs record the per file timings the split balances from.
Recording runs the suite in a single process, since durations only mean
anything when nothing else is competing, and uploads the file as an
artifact to be committed. No timings are committed with this change:
they should come from the runner they describe, so the first ones will
be recorded by this workflow.

Everything runs quarterly, and on demand. Quarterly is a compromise: the
timings only shift when the shape of the suite changes, so they do not
need refreshing often, and a stale file costs a worse split rather than
a wrong result. But a workflow nobody runs is a workflow that has
quietly stopped working, and the only other trigger here is a pull
request touching the parallel machinery, which may be months apart.

While the isolation work from #30184 is landing this will be red, which
is the point: it is the monitor for that work.

* test: give each worker its own stdout file and rubocop config

Three things the split needs from outside the rake task.

spec_helper redirects $stdout to a fixed path under the temporary directory. Several rspec processes then open the same file with mode "w" and truncate each other's output, so a failure reported by one worker could be overwritten by another. Name it per process instead, from TEST_ENV_NUMBER or the pid.

The plugin template's .rubocop.yml is generated and gitignored, so a working copy can be left holding one from an older fastlane. plugin_generator_spec then generates a plugin whose gemspec and rubocop config disagree about the Ruby version, which surfaces as `expected 0, got 1` with the rubocop output thrown away. Regenerating it before test_all and test_parallel is cheap and makes the run say the same thing on any machine.

And ignore the per worker logs and the raw timings the recording run writes.

* ci: split the suite on Windows too

Windows was the one platform the split had never run on, which left a gap in both of the things this workflow is for: it was neither being exercised for isolation there nor measured for speed.

Workers are spawned rather than forked, so there is nothing in the rake task that requires a Unix process model. The job mirrors the Linux one, minus the open file limit step, which has nothing to raise there. Recording gets its own job and its own timings file, since without Xcode the suite is a different shape again.

* ci: keep the worker logs when a split fails

The task prints which examples failed, but the reason is in the per worker log and that never leaves the runner. A split only failure cannot be reproduced without both the message and the bucket the worker was given, so upload the logs when the job fails.

* test: record each worker's split in a file of its own

The manifest that says which files a worker was given was written as a header in that worker's log, and the worker then appends to the same log through a redirect. On Windows the header does not survive that, so it came out empty exactly where it matters most: a split only failure cannot be reproduced without knowing what the worker ran.

Write it to rspec_worker_N.units instead, which nothing but the parent touches, and upload it alongside the logs.

Print the path rather than the contents. A worker carries over a hundred files and pasting them into a CI log buries the failures above it, so the report names the file and the command that expands it.

The log still has to be truncated before the worker starts. That used to happen as a side effect of writing the header into it, and without it a second run appends to the first and every count read back out is wrong.

* test: record the spec timings on the runners they balance

Recorded by the workflow's own jobs rather than on a laptop, one file per platform, each carrying where it came from:

  {"at": "2026-09-11", "ci": true, "runner": "GitHub Actions", "cores": 3, "ruby": "3.4.10", "xcode": "16.4"}

The three are different shapes, which is the reason they are separate files. macOS spends 558s, dominated by the scan specs that shell out to xcodebuild. Linux spends 106s, because those skip entirely, and its heaviest file is deliver's metadata upload. Windows spends 283s and is dominated by gradle and the crashlytics upload, neither of which is near the top anywhere else.

These balance the runners, not a developer machine. A 14 core laptop reading the 3 core macOS file predicts an even split and does not get one, because the relative cost of the files is not the same on both. Developers are better served by `rake spec_timings` on their own machine, or by the file size fallback.

* test: join the workers' rspec json into the one file a reporter reads

rspec's json formatter is how a run gets reported on CI, and a worker only ever sees its own slice of the suite. Each writes its own file and they are joined afterwards, so anything reading the result sees the whole run rather than a quarter of it.

The examples are concatenated and the counts added. The durations are not: they overlap, so their sum is not the wall clock and would report the run as slower than it was. The longest worker is kept instead, which is the closest honest answer. The join happens before the failure reporting, which aborts.

Only when GITHUB_ACTIONS is set, matching what `rake test_all` already does.

* docs: document the parallel split, the isolated home and the guards

Testing.md already covers running the suite, picking a file and chasing a flickering test. It does not cover what this work added: splitting the suite across processes, running it against a throwaway home directory, and the two guards that report state leaking between examples.

Also records the stale generated .rubocop.yml, which surfaces as a bare `expected 0, got 1` from plugin_generator_spec and looks like an environment problem rather than the stale file it is.

* docs: say where the seed comes from

Testing.md shows how to pass a seed back but never says where the number comes from, which leaves the most useful part of chasing an order dependent failure to be guessed at. A randomized run prints it twice, as it starts and as its last line.

Also note what a seed does not do. It pins the order, so a failure that depends on state outside the process reproduces on your machine and not on a colleague's whatever seed you use.

* docs: say that test_isolated covers TMPDIR too

commits.message:
build: refactoring our use of translate-c (#14203)

This commit refactors our use of translate-c, in preparation for larger
removal of `cImport` and better co-ordination between building of C
dependencies and translation of headers.

The major update is the creation of an internal helper package that
wraps our use of the external translate-c library. This allows us to not
only have better shorthand and a data-driven, declarative approach to C
translation (versus the otherwise more imperative approach), it also
funnels the external dependency into a single package instead of
spreading it out among what will be an increasingly larger amount of
places as dependencies in `pkg/` get updated.

It also includes some refactors, namely to the harfbuzz package, which
has had its individual settings refactored into helpers to allow for the
settings to be better shared between translation and the build of the
c-based static library.

Wuffs has also had a bit of a refactor too so that we don't generate a
file with all of the macro defines in it - we just send these in as `-D`
flags now.

Merge pull request #1355 from shorepine/amyboard-bus-distortion

AMYboard Web: add bus Distortion section (type / drive / mix)

AMYboard Web: add bus Distortion section (type / drive / mix)

AMY's distortion stage (amy docs/distortions.md) runs per bus, first in the
bus FX chain. Expose it in the editor's FX column next to EQ/Chorus/Reverb/
Echo as a Distortion section with three knobs:

- type: selection over off / clip / fold / clip+fold / crush / all. Each
  option sends one wire line carrying all three stage toggles
  (GC<c>GF<f>GH<bits>,<rate>) so the knob log keeps a single last-wins slot
  per bus. The bitcrusher rides a fixed 6 bits / hold 5 (the doc's demo
  setting); GH0,0 is off.
- drive: log knob 1/16..16 (GD), default 1.
- mix: 0..1 (GM), default 1.

Plumbing: selection knobs may now carry per-option wire fragments
(option_codes) in place of a numeric %v, and a no_cc flag keeps the CC editor
off knobs whose wire line isn't a value. Readback from AMY events maps a bus's
stage set onto the nearest type option and ignores G lines that name an osc,
so per-osc distortion in a patch doesn't move the bus knobs.

commits.message:
perf(grouping): return file indices instead of paths (#1209)

The grouping LLM call asked the model to echo full file paths back in its
JSON response, making the output size proportional to the sum of all path
lengths. On large change sets this overflowed the completion token limit;
the truncated JSON then failed to parse and the whole change set degraded to
per-file dispatch, multiplying downstream review calls.

Switch the grouping contract to integer indices:

- buildFileList prefixes each file with a zero-based index, e.g.
  "[0] MODIFIED path (+12/-3)".
- groupingResponse.Files is now []int; the model returns those indices.
- parseGroupingResponse maps indices back to diffs by position, skipping
  out-of-range indices (the index equivalent of the previous unknown-path
  skip) and duplicates. A parse failure still returns an error and the
  caller falls back to per-file dispatch, exactly as before.
- Prompts updated to ask for integer indices.

The response is now an order of magnitude smaller, so truncation on large
change sets becomes rare instead of common.

Because the grouping response is now indices, the session viewer resolves
them back to paths for display:

- buildGroupingIndex scans the request's numbered file list (user message
  only) to build an index->path map.
- parseGroupingGroups unmarshals the response into indices; a legacy
  path-string response reports not-ok so the viewer keeps showing the raw
  text (already readable for those older sessions).
- groupingView maps indices to paths and falls back to the raw response
  when nothing resolves (format drift), avoiding a wall of "#idx".
- The grouping card renders label + resolved paths with a collapsible raw
  response for audit. No on-disk format changes; existing sessions render
  retroactively.

repos.name: sparrowcode/PermissionsKit
repos.description: Universal API for request permission and get its statuses.

commits.message:
refactor: drop dead branches and unused imports across the permissions

EKAuthorizationStatusAuthorized is declared as an alias of fullAccess and
kCLAuthorizationStatusAuthorized as an alias of authorizedAlways, so in
Calendar, Reminders and Location the branch listed first swallowed the one
below it. Location now says plainly what it always did: always covers either
access level, when-in-use covers only its own.

Calendar and Location kept a Permission.Kind and unpacked it with switches
ending in fatalError, although each type only ever holds its own kind. They
store the access level instead and build the kind from it, which also lets
Calendar request the level directly rather than through two intermediate
closures.

The location handlers no longer implement locationManager(_:didChangeAuthorization:),
deprecated since iOS 14 and never called at the current deployment target.
Location imported EventKit instead of CoreLocation and Bluetooth imported
CloudKit without using it. The German strings file still carried nine keys
from an interface the package no longer ships.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

refactor: move microphone and photo library off deprecated APIs

AVAudioSession.recordPermission and requestRecordPermission are deprecated
since iOS 17 in favour of AVAudioApplication, with the old path kept for
iOS 15 and 16.

PHPhotoLibrary.authorizationStatus() and requestAuthorization(_:) carry
API_DEPRECATED_WITH_REPLACEMENT and, by Apple's own note, report plain
authorized even under limited access; both now go through the access level
variants, available since iOS 14.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: correct the Health usage keys, Chinese locale folder and Motion request

NSHealthShareUsageDescription describes reading samples and
NSHealthUpdateUsageDescription describes writing them, so the two keys were
returned by the wrong properties — apps copying them into Info.plist ended up
with swapped descriptions.

Simplified Chinese lived in zh_Hans.lproj with an underscore, which no bundle
ever matches; the folder is now zh-Hans.lproj like its Traditional sibling.

Motion called stopActivityUpdates() after a query, though that method pairs
with startActivityUpdates and did nothing here. The remaining trick — asking
for an empty date range purely to raise the dialog — is now explained.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

refactor: adopt Swift 6 language mode and remove the CocoaPods plumbing

The manifest moves to swift-tools-version 6.3 with swiftLanguageModes
[.v6], and the per-product PERMISSIONSKIT_* defines are gone — they only
existed to carve the sources into podspec subspecs, while SPM already
compiles every permission as its own target. Products and targets are now
derived from one list of permission names instead of sixteen identical
blocks.

In the sources that means the conditional import of the core module and
the gates that tested nothing but a define both collapse, Text.bundle
always resolves to .module, and the MIT header leaves all 23 files, as in
the other packages.

For strict concurrency the completion closures become @MainActor rather
than @Sendable: a permission dialog is UI work, and @Sendable would reject
the usual `request { [weak self] in ... }` from a view controller. They are
now called through Task { @MainActor in ... }, copied into a local first
where a delegate would otherwise send a non-Sendable handler; openSettingPage
is main actor isolated and drops its queue hop; the handler singletons are
marked nonisolated(unsafe), and the notification settings lookup keeps only
the Sendable authorization status behind its semaphore.

Also fixes the reqeustUpdate and Ovveride typos and renames the notification
options file that carried "userNotifcation" in its name.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

chore(repo): drop CocoaPods support and GitHub boilerplate

Match the layout of the other sparrowcode packages: no podspec, no issue
and pull request templates, no code of conduct or contributing guide.
README is rewritten in the same shape as DiffableKit and SwiftBoost —
description, installation, the permission table with its Info.plist keys,
and usage — and gitignore now covers .build.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

refactor(sources): drop code paths for now-unsupported OS versions

The raised deployment targets make every availability check below iOS 15,
tvOS 15 and watchOS 9 always true, so the legacy branches were dead code:

- BluetoothPermission: collapse the 13.1 / 13.0 / CBPeripheralManager
  cascade into CBCentralManager.authorization
- BluetoothHandler: same collapse, and read the authorization from the
  class property instead of the instance one deprecated in iOS 13.1,
  which also removes the separate visionOS branch
- LocationPermission, LocationAccuracy: drop the iOS 14 fallbacks and a
  nested os(iOS) check inside a file already gated on it
- Location handlers: unmark locationManagerDidChangeAuthorization and
  read authorizationStatus off the manager instead of the deprecated
  class method, collapsing the per-platform ifdefs
- NotificationAccess: announcement and timeSensitive no longer fall back
  to alert
- CameraPermission, TrackingPermission: drop the @available on the types

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

build(package): raise deployment targets to iOS 15, tvOS 15 and watchOS 9

Xcode 26 deprecates the older platform values in PackageDescription, so
`.watchOS(.v4)` warned at the manifest's swift-tools-version 5.9. Align
every floor with the oldest version Apple still supports, and match the
podspec to the manifest.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Update PhoneNumberKit to 5.0.9 and phone-number metadata 9.0.39, keeping the manifest and lockfile aligned.
